items.question: What is a C# delegate, and how do Func and Action differ from a custom delegate type?
items.answer: A delegate is a sealed Common Language Runtime (CLR) type that stores a method reference (and optionally a target object) whose parameter list and return type are compatible. Instantiating it binds a method group; invoking it calls that method. Func and Action are generic base class library (BCL) aliases for the common shapes. Custom delegates still matter when the type name is the contract — especially events — or when you need ref/out parameters that older Func overloads did not express cleanly.
followUps: Does the delegate signature include the return type?
What does variance allow when assigning methods to delegates?
items.sixtySeconds: Typed method pointer plus optional target. Func returns; Action is void. Custom type when the name is the API.

items.question: How does multicast invocation work, and what goes wrong if a handler throws?
items.answer: Combining delegates with + or += produces a multicast delegate. Raise walks the invocation list in subscription order, synchronously. If one handler throws, later handlers do not run unless you call GetInvocationList() and invoke each entry in a try/catch. That is the interview answer for a message fan-out that must still ack after a metrics handler fails.
followUps: How do you remove one handler without clearing the whole list?
items.sixtySeconds: Invocation list, left to right. One exception aborts the rest unless you iterate GetInvocationList yourself.

items.question: Why is event safer than a public delegate field on a long-lived consumer?
items.answer: A public delegate field lets any caller assign null, replace the list, or invoke it. event exposes only add and remove (+= and -=). The publisher still decides when to raise. On a hosted service that lives for days, a short-lived pipeline that += a handler and forgets -= keeps that pipeline graph reachable from the host. Unsubscribe in Dispose, or do not use instance events for process-wide buses.
followUps: When would you implement custom add/remove accessors?
items.sixtySeconds: event = add/remove only. Public field = anyone can wipe or fire. Leaks = publisher holds subscriber.

items.question: When do you pick a local function over a lambda?
items.answer: Local functions are named, can be recursive without a dummy assignment, can use yield return, can apply attributes, and are not converted to a delegate unless you pass them as one. Argument validation before an iterator or async body lives in the outer method; the local function holds the iterator. Lambdas always allocate a delegate (and often a closure class). static on either forbids capture.
followUps: Can a lambda contain yield return?
How does a static local function interact with captured variables?
items.sixtySeconds: Local function: named, yield, cheaper if not turned into a delegate. Lambda: inline callback for LINQ and events.

items.question: What did C# 14 add to extensions compared with this-parameter methods?
items.answer: Classic extensions are static methods with a this receiver, instance-only, methods-only. C# 14 extension blocks inside a static class declare instance members (methods, properties) and a second form with a type-only receiver for static methods, static properties, and operators. Both compile to static methods in Intermediate Language (IL). They never override real instance members. Interviewers want you to say properties and static extensions are new, not that this-methods vanished.
followUps: Can an extension property replace an instance property of the same name?
How do ref receivers work on structs?
items.sixtySeconds: C# 14: extension { } blocks, properties, static type members. Still lose to real members. this-methods still legal.

items.question: When does a lambda become an expression tree instead of a delegate?
items.answer: When the target type is Expression<TDelegate> and the body is a single expression — not a block. Entity Framework Core and other IQueryable providers walk that tree to emit SQL. A statement lambda or a lambda passed to IEnumerable always becomes IL plus an optional closure display class. Expecting EF to translate a block-bodied lambda is a common production bug that shows up as client evaluation warnings.
followUps: What is the difference between IQueryable and IEnumerable for lambdas?
Can you mix expression trees and delegates in one LINQ chain?
items.sixtySeconds: Expression<T> plus single expression body equals tree for IQueryable. Block body equals delegate only. EF needs trees.

items.question: Your RabbitMQ consumer metrics handler throws on one poison message — how do you keep ack running?
items.answer: Snapshot the event or delegate field to a local, call GetInvocationList(), and invoke each handler in its own try/catch. Log the failing handler name and continue. Do not use direct Invoke on the multicast delegate if fault isolation matters. This mirrors wrapping each addEventListener call in JavaScript try/catch. Production telemetry should record invocation list length versus handlers completed.
followUps: When would you replace in-process events with channels?
items.sixtySeconds: GetInvocationList, per-handler try/catch, snapshot field first. Metrics throw must not block ack.

items.question: How do static lambdas help on a high-concurrency cache factory path?
items.answer: A static lambda cannot capture locals, parameters, or instance members — the compiler emits no display class. On a hot GetOrCreateAsync factory that runs millions of times, a capturing lambda pins the request payload until the cache entry expires. Mark the factory static and pass data through the cache API instead. Prove the win with BenchmarkDotNet or dotnet-counters gen-0 before and after.
followUps: What does the compiler emit for a capturing lambda?
Is static local function equivalent to static lambda?
items.sixtySeconds: static lambda equals no closure class. Capturing pins request graph. Profile gen-0 on hot cache paths.

items.question: Compare C# delegates with JavaScript first-class functions in an interview.
items.answer: JavaScript functions are objects you pass freely. C# methods become values only when bound to Func, Action, or a custom delegate — the CLR enforces signatures at runtime. JavaScript EventTarget uses string event names; C# events are typed members. Multicast exception semantics match unless you isolate each handler. TypeScript function types erase; C# delegate types do not.
followUps: How does AbortSignal map to IDisposable unsubscribe?
Why does -= with a new lambda fail?
items.sixtySeconds: JS native functions. C# needs delegate type. Typed events. Same ref for unsubscribe. TS types erased.
